chapter_title: Inside the FPGA: LUTs, CLBs, and Programmable Interconnect
chapter_summary:
To understand how an FPGA works, you must look inside it. The fundamental building block of an FPGA is the **Look-Up Table (LUT)**. A LUT is a small memory (typically 16x1 for a 4-input LUT, or 64x1 for a 6-input LUT) that stores the truth table of a Boolean function. The inputs to the LUT serve as the address bits, and the output is the data bit stored at that address. For example, a 4-input LUT can implement any Boolean function of four variables because there are 2^4 = 16 possible input combinations, and the LUT can store a 0 or 1 for each combination.

Here is how a 4-input LUT implements an AND-OR function: suppose the function is F = (A AND B) OR (C AND D). The truth table has 16 rows. For each row where A=1, B=1, C=0, D=0, the output is 1 (because A AND B is true). The FPGA configuration tool calculates the truth table, stores it in the LUT's SRAM cells, and the LUT produces the correct output for any combination of inputs. The LUT itself is just a multiplexer connected to SRAM cells. The inputs A, B, C, and D select which SRAM cell drives the output. This means the LUT is a universal logic element — it can implement any function of its inputs, not just AND, OR, or XOR.

A LUT is typically combined with a **D flip-flop** and a **carry chain** to form a **Logic Element (LE)** or **Configurable Logic Block (CLB)**. In Intel terminology, this is called a Logic Element (LE). In Xilinx terminology, it is called a Slice. A single CLB contains:
- One or more LUTs (usually 4-input or 6-input)
- One or more D flip-flops (for sequential logic)
- A carry chain (for fast arithmetic operations like addition)
- A multiplexer to select between LUT output and flip-flop output
- Control signals for clock, enable, and asynchronous set/reset

The combination of a LUT and a flip-flop allows a CLB to implement either combinational logic (the LUT output feeds directly to the routing) or sequential logic (the LUT output feeds the flip-flop, and the flip-flop output feeds the routing). This is the basis of all digital design in FPGAs: combinational logic computes the next state, and sequential logic stores it.

The **programmable interconnect** is the network of wires that connects CLBs to each other and to the I/O blocks. It is the most complex and area-consuming part of the FPGA. The interconnect consists of horizontal and vertical routing channels with wires of different lengths (short wires for local connections, long wires for global connections). At the intersections of these channels are **switch matrices**, which contain programmable switches that can connect any wire to any other wire. The switch matrix is what makes the FPGA "field programmable" — by changing the configuration of the switches, you can create any wiring topology.

The interconnect is also the biggest performance bottleneck in an FPGA. A signal may pass through multiple switch matrices and wire segments, each adding delay. The longest path through the combinational logic and interconnect determines the maximum clock frequency of the design. This is why **static timing analysis** is critical: the tool must verify that every signal arrives at its destination before the next clock edge.

Modern FPGAs also contain **specialized hard blocks** that are not programmable but are pre-designed for specific functions:
- **Block RAM (BRAM):** Dedicated memory blocks, typically 18 Kb or 36 Kb, used for FIFOs, buffers, and lookup tables.
- **Digital Signal Processing (DSP) blocks:** Pre-designed multipliers and accumulators for fast arithmetic.
- **Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs):** Clock generation and frequency synthesis circuits.
- **High-speed transceivers:** Serial communication blocks for PCIe, Ethernet, and other protocols.
- **I/O blocks:** Configurable input/output cells that support various voltage standards (LVCMOS, LVDS, HSTL, SSTL).

screens.title: Inside the FPGA: LUTs, CLBs & Programmable Interconnect
screens.subtitle: How memory-backed LUTs, logic blocks, and routed wires form a flexible, field-programmable chip

narration.text: In this chapter you will open the FPGA and see the building blocks that make reprogrammable logic possible. We'll start with the Look-Up Table, a tiny memory that stores a truth table and behaves like any combinational logic function. From there we'll combine LUTs with flip-flops and carry chains inside a configurable logic block to implement both combinational and sequential circuits. Finally, we'll explore the programmable interconnect: the grid of routing channels and switch matrices that wire every block together, and why routing dominates area and delay on the chip. As you learn, notice two recurring themes: the LUT is universal because it stores a function directly, and the interconnect is the bottleneck because every routed signal traverses programmable switches that add delay. A concrete example you will follow is how a four-input function is stored in a 16-entry LUT and how a simple XOR tree maps to multiple LUTs. By the end you'll understand not just the parts, but how they interact — which helps you optimize placement, choose when to use hard blocks like BRAM or DSP, and reason about timing. Consider how storing a truth table differs from wiring fixed gates, and how that difference makes FPGAs programmable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to explain, describe, and apply

narration.text: By the end of these screens you will be able to explain how a Look-Up Table implements any combinational Boolean function by storing a truth table and using its inputs as address bits. You will describe the structure of a Configurable Logic Block or Logic Element, including the role of the LUT, flip-flop, and carry chain. You will also be able to explain how the programmable interconnect — horizontal and vertical routing channels and switch matrices — moves signals between blocks, and why that interconnect is the largest contributor to area and delay in an FPGA. Each objective pairs a concept with a practical reason. For example, understanding LUT truth tables lets you map functions efficiently and count required LUTs. Knowing CLB internals helps you decide where to place registers to meet timing. And understanding interconnect delays leads directly to timing-driven placement and routing. As you learn, test your comprehension by drawing a small truth table, mapping it to a LUT, and tracing a signal across two switch matrices. That simple practice connects theory to the placement and timing decisions you'll make in real designs.

screens.title: Look-Up Table (LUT): Truth table as memory
screens.subtitle: How inputs become addresses and how a LUT implements any combinational function

narration.text: A Look-Up Table is best understood as a tiny memory that holds a function's truth table. For a 4-input LUT you have 16 memory locations, one for each possible input combination. Each input vector becomes an address. The LUT reads the stored bit for that address and drives the output. This is not a network of fixed gates; it is data-driven logic. Concretely, if the function is F equals A AND B OR C AND D, the synthesis tool computes the output for each of the 16 input rows and writes a 0 or 1 into each SRAM cell. At runtime the input bits select the stored cell and the LUT outputs the precomputed value. This makes LUTs universal: any Boolean function of the inputs can be programmed simply by writing the correct bits. A common misconception is to think a LUT is a reusable gate like an AND — instead, think of it as writable memory that behaves like a gate once configured. Example practice: draw the truth table for a 2-input XOR and see how those four bits map to a 2-input LUT. Takeaway: treating the LUT as stored truth table clarifies why complex functions map to combinations of LUTs and why LUT input count limits how many inputs a single LUT can handle.

keyIdea.title: LUT definition
keyIdea.text: The LUT stores a function's truth table in SRAM; inputs select the stored entry and produce the output, making the LUT a universal combinational element.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LUT: Truth table
Definition
A small SRAM-based table where input bits address stored outputs.
Key points
  • For n inputs the LUT has 2^n stored entries.
  • Inputs act as the address to select the output bit.
  • LUTs are universal: any combinational function of the inputs can be stored.
  • A LUT is implemented as SRAM cells feeding a multiplexer network.
Key Takeaway

Think of the LUT as a programmable truth table: inputs choose the stored output rather than composing fixed gates.

Concrete example
F = (A AND B) OR (C AND D) implemented in a 4-input LUT. The synthesis tool computes the 16 output bits and stores them in the SRAM cells. At runtime A,B,C,D address the correct stored bit.
2-input XOR truth table (mapping exercise)
Inputs: A,B. Rows: 00→0, 01→1, 10→1, 11→0. These four bits fill a 2-input LUT's memory.
Common misconception: a LUT is not a fixed gate network. It stores output values for each input combination, so complex functions are just different stored patterns, not new wiring.

screens.title: LUT Internal: SRAM cells and multiplexer
screens.subtitle: How the LUT uses SRAM and a multiplexer tree to present the stored bit as the output

narration.text: Inside the LUT the stored truth table lives in SRAM cells, and a multiplexer network selects the correct cell based on the input address. Conceptually, each possible input vector indexes a memory cell that holds a single 0 or 1. The input bits feed decoder logic that chooses which SRAM output is forwarded. This is usually implemented as a small multiplexer tree so that the selected stored bit drives the LUT output. The important practical point is that implementation is memory-driven rather than gate-composed. For example, a 4-input LUT has 16 SRAM bits. When inputs match one of the 16 addresses, the corresponding bit flows through the multiplexer and becomes the logic output. A common misconception is to think the LUT recomputes logic using gates; instead, it reads precomputed results. This design lets FPGA tools implement arbitrary Boolean functions without changing silicon. As a short exercise, imagine flipping a single SRAM bit to change the function for one input row — that demonstrates programmability. Takeaway: knowing the LUT is an SRAM plus multiplexer helps you reason about size, power, and how complex many-input functions map into multiple LUTs.

keyIdea.title: LUT internals
keyIdea.text: The LUT combines SRAM cells that store output bits with a multiplexer tree that selects the addressed bit as output.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › LUT Internals
Architecture snapshot
SRAM cells store one bit per input vector; a multiplexer tree selects the stored bit based on input signals.
SRAM array: 2^n bits
Multiplexer decoder
Address inputs
Single output bit
Practical note: changing one SRAM cell changes output for only one input combination — this is the essence of programmability.
Concrete mapping example
A 4-input function requires 16 SRAM bits. The inputs A,B,C,D form a 4-bit address. The LUT multiplexer routes the accessed SRAM cell to the output. No gate restructuring is necessary.
Common misconception

A LUT is not a fixed network of gates; it's programmed by writing memory bits, then the multiplexer returns the stored value for given inputs.

screens.title: Function count and truth-table scaling
screens.subtitle: How many different Boolean functions a LUT can implement and why size matters

narration.text: A useful quantitative fact is how many distinct Boolean functions a LUT with n inputs can realize. Each input vector corresponds to an addressable SRAM bit, and those bits can be independently zero or one. Therefore a LUT with n inputs has 2^n addressable rows and each row can be 0 or 1, yielding 2^(2^n) possible distinct functions. For a 4-input LUT this evaluates to 2^(16) or 65,536 different functions. This large number explains why a single LUT is powerful: with only a few bits you can represent many possible behaviors. But the count also shows a practical limit: as the number of inputs grows, the internal memory size and complexity climb exponentially, so vendors choose typical LUT sizes like 4 or 6 inputs for practical trade-offs. A common misconception is mixing up 2^n (input combinations) with 2^(2^n) (number of functions). Example: a 2-input LUT has 4 rows and therefore 2^4 = 16 possible functions. Takeaway: function count gives perspective on LUT universality and helps you reason about why designs split complex logic across multiple LUTs when input counts exceed a single LUT's width.

keyIdea.title: Function scaling
keyIdea.text: An n-input LUT supports 2^(2^n) distinct functions; for n=4 that is 65,536 possibilities, illustrating the LUT's universality but also why LUT input size is limited.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Function Count
Counting idea
Each of the 2^n input combinations maps to a stored bit. Every different assignment of those bits defines a distinct Boolean function.
Formula: functions = 2^(2^n)
Example: n = 4 → 2^(2^4) = 2^16 = 65,536 possible functions for a 4-input LUT.
Practical implications
  • Large function space gives LUT power to implement arbitrary logic patterns.
  • But supporting many inputs grows memory size exponentially, so vendors limit input width.
  • Complex functions with many inputs are split across multiple LUTs in synthesis.
Misconception check

Don't confuse number of input combinations (2^n) with number of possible functions (2^(2^n)).

screens.title: Configurable Logic Block (CLB / LE)
screens.subtitle: How LUTs, flip-flops, carry chains, and muxes combine to form programmable logic elements

narration.text: A Configurable Logic Block or Logic Element groups several primitives to implement both combinational and sequential behavior. At minimum a CLB contains one or more LUTs to compute combinational results, one or more D flip-flops to store state, and a carry chain for fast arithmetic. There's also an output multiplexer that chooses whether the CLB drives routing from the raw LUT output or from the flip-flop output. Control signals such as clock, enable, and asynchronous set or reset allow designers to manage timing and synchronous behavior. The practical significance is that the CLB is where logic is mapped: combinational computations happen in the LUT and, when needed, their results are registered by the flip-flop for sequential circuits. For example, to implement a simple register you program the LUT to compute the next state and route that into the flip-flop; the flip-flop then drives the routed signal. A common misconception is that LUTs alone provide storage: they do not. Storage comes from the D flip-flop. Takeaway: understanding CLB internals helps you decide where to insert registers to break timing-critical paths and how arithmetic primitives like the carry chain speed adders inside the block.

keyIdea.title: CLB composition
keyIdea.text: A CLB combines LUTs, D flip-flops, carry chains, and an output mux to support both combinational and sequential logic with control signals.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Configurable Logic Block
CLB components
  • LUTs: compute combinational outputs.
  • D flip-flops: store state for sequential logic.
  • Carry chain: fast path for arithmetic carry propagation.
  • Output mux: selects registered or combinational output.
  • Control signals: clock, enable, async set/reset.
Understanding which output the mux chooses and when to register results is central to placement and timing decisions.
Concrete scenario
Suppose you compute next_state in the LUT and want it stored on the clock edge. Route the LUT output into the CLB flip-flop. The flip-flop output then drives downstream routing. This pattern separates combinational computation from state storage.
Misconception

The LUT does not provide storage by itself; flip-flops in the CLB provide the register semantics.

screens.title: Combinational vs Sequential use of a CLB
screens.subtitle: When the LUT output goes directly to routing and when it goes through a flip-flop

narration.text: CLBs support two primary modes of use. In combinational mode the LUT output drives the routing fabric directly. The LUT computes a logic result based solely on current inputs and that result propagates immediately through the interconnect. In sequential mode the LUT's output feeds a D flip-flop inside the CLB, and the flip-flop's registered output then drives routing. This registered path aligns logic activity to the clock and creates predictable timing boundaries. A simple process to decide which mode to use: if the output needs to be sampled synchronously at a clock edge or used as state, route it into the flip-flop. If the result is purely combinational and timing is not constrained by a register boundary, allow the LUT to drive routing directly. Example: implement a one-bit state machine where the LUT computes next_state and the flip-flop stores current_state on each clock; the LUT output must go into the flip-flop. A common misconception is that registering everywhere hurts performance; while registers add clock-cycle latency, adding registers can reduce combinational path length and improve maximum clock frequency. Takeaway: use CLB flip-flops strategically to meet timing and express sequential behavior.

keyIdea.title: CLB modes
keyIdea.text: Use LUT output directly for combinational logic; feed the LUT into the CLB flip-flop when state or synchronous sampling is required.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Combinational vs Sequential
When to use combinational output
Use when the value is purely a combinational result and does not need to be sampled on a clock edge.
Direct routing reduces latency but increases combinational path length for timing analysis.
When to register (sequential)
Route the LUT output into the flip-flop when you need synchronous sampling, state storage, or shorter timing segments between registers.
Key Takeaway

Strategic registering reduces critical path length and helps meet timing, even though it introduces one-cycle latency.

screens.title: Carry Chain: fast arithmetic inside CLBs
screens.subtitle: Why carry chains exist and how they speed addition compared to general routing

narration.text: Carry chains are dedicated wired paths within CLBs optimized for arithmetic carry propagation. Adding numbers requires carries to flow from less significant bits to more significant bits. If carries were routed through the general programmable interconnect, each carry would traverse switch matrices and incur extra delay. The carry chain provides a local, fast path that links adjacent CLBs or logic elements so that carries move quickly with minimal switching overhead. This optimization yields much faster adders and arithmetic operations than synthesizing carries through arbitrary routing. For instance, when implementing an adder the synthesis tool uses the carry chain to connect bit slices so the carry from one bit is available to the next with small incremental delay. A common misconception is that all inter-CLB communication is equal; carry chains are purposely faster and affect how you map arithmetic. Takeaway: when your design needs high-performance addition or accumulation, rely on the vendor's carry chain support rather than generic LUT-based ripple methods because the carry chain reduces delay and area for arithmetic paths. Carry Chain: fast arithmetic inside CLBs means carry chains provide a low-delay path for arithmetic carries between adjacent logic slices, enabling fast adders and accumulators.. In practical terms, why carry chains exist and how they speed addition compared to general routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Carry chain purpose
keyIdea.text: Carry chains provide a low-delay path for arithmetic carries between adjacent logic slices, enabling fast adders and accumulators.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Carry Chain
What it is
A hardware path optimized for carrying the arithmetic carry signal between adjacent bit-slices, avoiding full routing overhead.
Low delay links
Local routing inside CLB
Used for adders and MACs
Example: synthesis maps adder bits to adjacent slices and uses the carry chain so carries propagate quickly from bit 0 up to bit n with minimal extra switching delay.
Misconception
Not all inter-CLB connections are equal: carry chains are intentionally faster and specialized for arithmetic paths.
Key Takeaway

Use vendor carry-chain primitives when you need high-performance adds rather than relying on general routing between LUTs.

screens.title: Programmable interconnect: channels and switch matrices
screens.subtitle: How wires of different lengths and programmable switches form the routing fabric

narration.text: The programmable interconnect is the network of wires and programmable switches that connects CLBs, input and output blocks, and hard blocks across the FPGA. It is organized into horizontal and vertical routing channels. Each channel contains wires of different lengths: short wires that span nearby blocks for local connections and longer wires that span many blocks for global connections. At regular intersections are switch matrices — arrays of programmable switches that can connect any incoming wire to chosen outgoing wires. These switch matrices are configured in the bitstream so that the overall routing topology implements your netlist. The interconnect is the most complex and area-consuming part of the chip because it must support many possible wiring topologies. A signal sent from a source CLB to a distant destination may traverse several wire segments and switch matrices, and each segment and switch adds delay. Example: a signal routed across a moderate distance might pass through three switch matrices and two long wire segments, each contributing to the path delay. Misconception: people sometimes assume logic is the dominant cost; in modern FPGAs the routing fabric occupies more area and determines achievable clock frequency. Takeaway: routing choices and switch settings are central to placement and timing closure.

keyIdea.title: Interconnect basics
keyIdea.text: Routing channels of varied wire lengths plus switch matrices form a programmable fabric; routing choices determine delay and area usage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Programmable Interconnect
Routing architecture
Horizontal and vertical channels contain multiple wires of varied lengths. Switch matrices at intersections provide programmable connectivity between wire segments.
Short wires: local links
Medium wires: regional spans
Long wires: global routes
Concrete impact
Each switch and wire segment adds delay. A long routed net will typically traverse multiple switch matrices and wire segments, and that cumulative delay can dominate the critical path.
Warning

Routing is the main bottleneck for timing. Pay attention to placement and the number of switch matrices a net crosses.

screens.title: Wire length choices: short vs long wires
screens.subtitle: How wire length impacts connection options, area and timing

narration.text: Routing channels typically contain a mix of short, medium, and long wires. Short wires span nearby CLBs and are efficient for local connections with low delay. Medium wires cover several blocks, letting nets hop regionally without touching many switch matrices. Long wires span large parts of the chip and are intended for global signals, but their use comes at a cost: they occupy more routing resources and can introduce larger skew if used indiscriminately. The design trade-off is clear: prefer short wires for local signals and reserve long wires for nets that genuinely need wide reach. For example, a clock or global reset might justify long wires or dedicated clock networks, but a combinational signal between neighboring logic should use short wires to minimize delay. A misconception is to think a longer wire is always better for reach; in fact, routing tools balance wire type and switch usage to minimize delay and congestion. Takeaway: understanding wire types helps you interpret routing reports and direct placement to keep critical nets local and reduce switch-matrix crossings that increase delay. Wire length choices: short vs long wires means short wires are low-delay for local connections; long wires reach far but cost area and timing. keep critical nets local when possible.. In practical terms, how wire length impacts connection options, area and timing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wire trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Short wires are low-delay for local connections; long wires reach far but cost area and timing. Keep critical nets local when possible.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Wire Lengths
Short wires
Used for neighboring CLBs, minimal switch crossings, low delay and low area per connection.
Best for: local combinational signals and short data paths.
Long wires
Span large distances with fewer hops but occupy larger routing resources and can add skew or delay if misused.
Best for: global signals and nets that must cross many regions.
Practical guideline
  • Keep timing-critical nets local to avoid multiple switch matrices.
  • Reserve long wires for signals that must reach across the device.
  • Interpret routing congestion and delay reports to adjust placement.

screens.title: Hard blocks: BRAM, DSP, PLL, transceivers, I/O
screens.subtitle: Dedicated, pre-designed resources that offload common functions from the fabric

narration.text: Modern FPGAs integrate specialized hard blocks to implement common, resource-heavy functions more efficiently than programmable fabric alone. Block R A M, or BRAM, provides dedicated memory blocks — for FIFOs, line buffers, and small lookup tables — that are larger and more area-efficient than building equivalent memory from LUTs. DSP blocks include pre-designed multipliers and accumulators optimized for arithmetic workloads and are much faster and smaller than composing arithmetic from general LUTs and carry chains. Phase-Locked Loops generate and synthesize clock frequencies, while high-speed transceivers implement serial protocols like PCIe or Ethernet and are built as hardened logic to meet timing and signaling standards. input and output blocks support various voltage standards and protect signals at the package boundary. The practical implication is to prefer hard blocks when you need large memory, high-throughput arithmetic, or reliable high-speed serial links; synthesizing these functions into general fabric is possible but inefficient. A common misconception is that hard blocks are optional niceties; in many designs using DSPs or BRAM is essential for performance and efficient resource usage. Takeaway: use hard blocks where they map directly to your workload to save fabric resources and improve performance.

keyIdea.title: Hard blocks role
keyIdea.text: Hard blocks provide dedicated, efficient implementations of memory, arithmetic, clocking and high-speed I/O that outperform mapped fabric equivalents.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hard Blocks
Block RAM (BRAM)
Dedicated memory blocks for FIFOs, buffers, and large lookup tables that are more efficient than LUT-built memory.
DSP blocks
Pre-designed multipliers and accumulators optimized for fast arithmetic and reduce fabric usage for heavy math.
PLLs & Transceivers
Clock synthesis and high-speed serial links are hardened to meet timing and signal integrity requirements.
When to use them
If your design requires large memory, intensive DSP operations, or reliable high-speed IO, prefer hard blocks because they save LUT resources and improve performance and timing predictability.

screens.title: Mapping XORs into LUTs — a small exercise
screens.subtitle: Store the 2-input XOR truth table and reason how many 4-input LUTs form a 4-input XOR

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete hands-on activity that appears in the chapter. Start with the 2-input XOR: F equals A XOR B. Its truth table has four rows: 00→0, 01→1, 10→1, 11→0. A 2-input LUT stores these four bits in its SRAM cells so that the input pair addresses the correct stored bit. Now expand to a 4-input XOR, F equals A XOR B XOR C XOR D. One efficient way to implement this is a tree of 2-input XORs: compute X1 equals A XOR B, X2 equals C XOR D, then F equals X1 XOR X2. Each 2-input XOR fits into one 2-input LUT, so the tree requires three 2-input LUTs. If your device has 4-input LUTs, each 2-input XOR still fits in one 4-input LUT with unused inputs, so you end up using three 4-input LUTs as well. A common misconception is thinking a single larger LUT can always absorb the whole function; a 4-input XOR is within a 4-input LUT's input width, but because of synthesis patterns and optimization, tools may still choose a tree pattern depending on available resources and timing. Takeaway: map functions by counting needed input coverage and consider how synthesis will pack small functions into wider LUT primitives.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: A 2-input XOR maps to one small LUT; a 4-input XOR implemented as a tree of three 2-input XORs requires three LUTs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on XOR Mapping
2-input XOR truth table
00 → 0
01 → 1
10 → 1
11 → 0
These four stored bits fill a 2-input LUT's SRAM. The inputs address the correct row to produce the XOR result.
4-input XOR as a tree
Compute X1 = A XOR B, X2 = C XOR D, then F = X1 XOR X2. Each 2-input XOR is one LUT, so the tree uses three LUTs.
Key Takeaway

Map functions by counting input coverage and let synthesis pack small logic into available LUT widths. For a 4-input XOR, three 2-input XOR primitives are commonly used in a tree.

Quick practice
Draw the truth table for A XOR B XOR C and map how many 2-input XORs you need when forming a balanced tree. Notice how grouping affects depth and number of LUTs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders of the chapter's core ideas

narration.text: Let's summarize the essentials you should carry forward. First, a Look-Up Table stores a function's truth table in SRAM and uses inputs as addresses — this makes the LUT a universal combinational building block. Second, Configurable Logic Blocks combine LUTs, flip-flops, and carry chains so you can build both combinational and sequential circuits; use flip-flops to break timing-critical paths and carry chains to speed arithmetic. Third, the programmable interconnect, consisting of varied-length wires and switch matrices, is the dominant area and timing factor in FPGAs; routing choices determine how often signals cross switch matrices and therefore how much delay is introduced. Keep these three concepts in mind when you map logic, choose where to register signals, and decide whether to use hard blocks like BRAM or DSP for efficiency. A quick reflective question: when a path fails timing, would adding a register or changing routing be the better first step? That reflection ties the chapter's ideas into practical troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: LUT = stored truth table; CLB = LUT + flip-flop + carry chain; interconnect = routing fabric that sets performance limits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Concepts
Look-Up Table (LUT)
Stores the truth table in SRAM; inputs select the stored output bit, enabling arbitrary combinational functions.
Configurable Logic Block
Combines LUTs, flip-flops, and carry chains; supports both combinational outputs and registered state.
Programmable Interconnect
Routing channels and switch matrices connect blocks; routing choices and wire lengths dominate area and delay.
Summary takeaway
Remember these three building blocks when optimizing designs: store complex logic in LUTs, use CLB registers to manage timing, and reduce routing distance to improve clock speed.

screens.title: Quick Reference Cards
screens.subtitle: Three single-line concept cards to recall during design

narration.text: These three reference cards are short prompts to use while designing. Card one: LUT equals truth table in SRAM — use this to reason about how functions map to hardware. Card two: CLB equals logic plus registers and carry — use this when choosing where to place registers or arithmetic. Card three: routing equals delay and area — always inspect how many switch matrices a critical net must traverse. Use this strip as a quick checklist: count LUT inputs, check whether a register should break a long combinational path, and examine routing hops for critical nets. This quick-memory approach helps you make faster placement and optimization choices when iterating on your design.
